gates.reason: Inspected transcript-input distillation, command/path parsing, remote-target validation, and shell classification. The file treats inputs as data, performs no command execution or filesystem writes, and contains no network/LLM egress sink.
Correction mining can label unrelated files as a failed-to-fixed path correction based solely on matching non-generic filename stems.
Inspected the ingest and calculation hot paths. Shell and edit analysis have explicit per-command and per-transcript budgets, and aggregation passes are bounded linear scans of parsed calls.

findings.title: Filename-stem matching can fabricate file-path correction recommendations
findings.what: mineCorrections treats the first nearby successful same-tool call as a correction whenever its path has the same distinctive stem as the failed path. Stem equality does not establish file identity: for example, a failed Read of `packages/a/UserService.ts` followed by a successful Read of `packages/b/UserService.js` is emitted as a correction even though the files may be unrelated. The emitted recommendation therefore lacks reproducible evidence that the second path fixed the first operation.
findings.fix: Require a stronger path-identity relation before emitting a correction, such as one normalized path being a relative/suffix form of the other, or retain and validate explicit error/target provenance. Suppress the fact when identity cannot be established from available fields.
findings.acceptance: A focused test supplies a failed file-tool call for `packages/a/UserService.ts` followed within the window by a successful same-tool call for `packages/b/UserService.js` and asserts that no CorrectionFact is emitted; genuine relative-versus-absolute wrong-path retries remain detected.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial re-read confirmed that lines 4856-4866 validate only tool name, success state, unequal paths, and exact stem equality before lines 4868-4875 emit the correction. The generic-stem filter at lines 4794-4828 does not prevent collisions between distinct files with the same distinctive stem.
